item.title: Growth versus equity in a stochastic multiplicative wealth model: The cost of redistribution and the emergence of an inequality Laffer curve
item.description: arXiv:2611.27993v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A stochastic multiplicative wealth model with taxation and redistribution is extended to include two channels through which fiscal policy can reduce the economy's average growth rate: productive disincentive (a tax-dependent mean return) and administrative inefficiency (loss of part of the collected revenue). For uniform redistribution, the stationary density of normalized wealth remains an inverse-gamma law, but its shape parameter acquires a richer dependence on the tax rate. The central finding is the emergence of an "inequality Laffer curve": when the disincentive is sufficiently strong, the Gini coefficient first decreases, reaches a minimum at a finite tax rate, and then increases again as taxation intensifies. In the extreme limit the stationary state collapses back to the condensed phase, restoring the oligarchic transition. Both channels also create a direct trade-off between inequality and long-run average wealth, giving rise to a welfare-maximizing tax rate. The two channels are combined into a single analytically tractable model, and all predictions are validated by agent-based simulations. The results show that the qualitative existence of an optimal tax rate is robust whenever the aggregate growth rate responds to fiscal policy, while the inequality Laffer curve is a specific prediction of the productive-disincentive channel.
item.dc:creator: Renato Vieira dos Santos

item.title: Echoes of the boom in hydraulic fracturing: What changes in Louisiana's energy complex reveal about global energy cycles
item.description: arXiv:2611.28309v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The expansion of hydraulic fracturing (i.e. fracking) led to global shifts in energy markets that were felt acutely along the US Gulf Coast and particularly in the state of Louisiana. This article presents a data-focused examination of trends in the energy industry, and shows how they led to potentially counterintuitive, negative impacts in Louisiana's economy. Most notably, hydraulic fracturing led to a massive expansion in oil and gas supplies that contributed to a significant decline in oil prices in late 2014, contributing to significant job losses. Louisiana's economic downturns were tied to global shifts in energy markets that had major geostrategic implications. More broadly, results indicate that large and long period cycles in the supply, demand and price of oil can have widespread impacts on job creation and loss. In states like Louisiana with a large and diversified energy complex, the impacts of these trends can be highly uneven. One impact in the 21st Century appears to be highly concentrated areas of industrial development within a broader pattern of regional economic decline. Furthermore, trends identified in this study suggest the potential for the emergence of major cycles in the gas market. Whereas natural gas was previously mostly transported by pipelines and sold through long-term contracts, the emergence of liquified natural gas creates the potential for more volatile gas market dynamics. The implications of gas market cycles, while not yet known, could be of major economic significance.
item.dc:creator: Alexander S. Kolker, Robert Habans, Trey Cowan

item.title: What the annual energy balance hides: the coordination value of digital platforms for positive energy districts
item.description: arXiv:2611.29485v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Positive energy districts (PEDs) are usually assessed by annual net energy, whereas distribution networks operate hour by hour. An annually positive district still imports on low-generation hours and exports or curtails on high-generation hours. How large this hourly imbalance is behind an annual balance, and how much of it coordination among prosumers can close without new physical capacity, is not established. This paper models a multi-carrier prosumer community coupling electricity and heat behind a shared grid connection with a net-export hosting limit. The model is solved as a centralized community problem and as a price-taking peer-to-peer (P2P) market. Under convexity, the equilibrium implements the regularized community optimum and the P2P and congestion prices are the duals of the pool-clearing and hosting constraints. The model is calibrated to six European district archetypes with constructed hourly profiles. Hourly self-sufficiency is only 48-50% in the four deeply studied districts and ranges from 48-55% across all six, leaving a no-platform coordination gap of 2.8-5.9% of no-platform economic cost. The shared-forecast step recovers only 6-18% of the gap, while grid-aware pricing reduces curtailment by 45% in the primary district. Coordination mainly reduces surplus-side inefficiency, whereas closing the deficit side requires storage. The results are scenario-based projections for calibrated archetypes, and the operating benefit is small and contingent on binding hosting limits and high feed-in remuneration. For regulators and distribution system operators this supports hourly, bidirectional indicators alongside the annual positive-energy target, and a congestion charge active only in binding hours with a predetermined refund, while the business case for a platform at district scale rests on grid-side value and aggregation across districts.
item.dc:creator: Arega Getaneh Abate, Per Sieverts Nielsen, Xiufeng Liu, Brian O'Regan, Gerfried Cebrat, Cigdem Karadag, Valentina Zaccaria, Yang Liu, Madalin Silion, Ami Vadiee, Jakob Jespersen, Mahmut Sami Buker, Maria Simona Raboaca, Avinash Renuke, Betul Erdor Turk, Dudle Stewart

item.title: How to Mismatch Consumers
item.description: arXiv:2611.29502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Should a platform show all consumers all products, or at least those they like most? Or could it raise consumer surplus by mismatching some consumers: showing them only less-preferred products or even excluding them from trade? I show that in both monopoly and duopoly, mismatching can raise aggregate consumer surplus by inducing lower prices. In duopoly, consumer-optimal matching uses a cutoff policy: along each diagonal of equal valuation differences, consumers with lower valuations are matched only to less-preferred products, and some may subsequently be excluded. With independent uniform valuations, this raises aggregate consumer surplus by about 41% over full matching.
item.dc:creator: Wenhao Li

item.title: Neighbourhood flood damage amplifies mortgage default cascades
item.description: arXiv:2611.29652v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Floods threaten mortgage repayment by damaging homes, disrupting incomes, and worsening conditions in surrounding neighbourhoods. However, it remains unclear how these neighbourhood effects turn local damage into systemic mortgage distress, as Europe's housing crisis leaves households that lose their homes with few affordable alternatives. Using an agent-based model calibrated to Limburg, the Netherlands, we show that damage to surrounding properties can trigger mortgage defaults among households that can still afford to pay, including those whose own homes remain undamaged. In the most severe flood scenario, the annual foreclosure rate more than doubles. As each foreclosure lowers the value of nearby homes, it triggers a cascade. Floods make such large foreclosure cascades more frequent, with the share of foreclosures that belong to these cascades rising from 31% to 45%. They also shift foreclosures towards younger mortgages, when more debt is still outstanding. These findings show how neighbourhood damage extends mortgage risk beyond directly flooded homes and causes foreclosures to arrive in concentrated waves earlier in repayment.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Valle, Drona Kandhai, Cees Diks, Debraj Roy

item.title: Do Candlestick Charts Suffice? The Incremental Economic Value of Technical Indicators in Stock Return Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.30584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although technical analysis remains widely used in practice, the need for manually constructed indicators is increasingly questioned as deep learning models can extract features directly from OHLC price data. This paper examines the standalone economic value of trading volume and manually constructed technical-indicator groups and whether adding these groups to OHLC candlestick charts provides incremental economic value. Using daily data for 1,707 Chinese A-share stocks from 2013 to 2025, we construct approximately 3.36 million stock-window samples and encode them as multi-channel images containing candlestick charts, trading volume, and seven widely used manually constructed technical indicators. The primary analysis uses a 2D CNN on these images; complementary tests apply a logistic regression, a 1D CNN, and an LSTM to numerical representations of the same samples. Out-of-sample performance from 2021 to 2025 is evaluated using decile portfolios, Sharpe ratios, Fama--French alphas, and formal pairwise tests. Our empirical results yield two central findings. First, specifications based separately on OHLC, trading volume, and each technical-indicator group produce significantly positive high-minus-low returns and factor-adjusted alphas, together with economically meaningful Sharpe ratios; the OHLC-only specifications generally perform best under the nonlinear models. Second, adding these technical-indicator groups to OHLC does not systematically improve any of these performance measures in our setting. Together, these results provide the first large-scale evidence from the Chinese A-share market on the standalone and incremental economic value of these technical-indicator groups across multiple representations and model architectures.
item.dc:creator: Peng Liu, Yanyan Zheng

item.title: The Private Production of Safety Outside Options and the Burden of Protection
item.description: arXiv:2611.30735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protective interventions are typically evaluated by their ability to prevent harm. Yet protection also raises a distinct question: who bears the burden of adjusting to violence? I examine this allocation of protective adjustment using four randomized interventions in the United States. An offer of permanent housing assistance increases separation from a baseline partner combined with stable independent housing by 12.52 percentage points. Assignment to active police-response protocols reduces observed victim-only departures and increases suspect-only departures. Assignment to an emergency protection order increases documented directions for suspects to leave. These findings reveal two margins of the same allocation problem: housing assistance expands victims' ability to establish an independent residence, while enforcement shifts displacement obligations toward suspects. Protective policies thus shape not only the opportunities for safety, but also the distribution of the costs required to achieve it.
item.dc:creator: Elena Pisanelli

item.title: AI-Assisted Programming and Labor Demand
item.description: arXiv:2611.31083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI has demonstrated human-level performance on technical work tasks, yet evidence on how these task-level capabilities are changing labor demand remains scarce. We study the firm-level adoption of GitHub Copilot, an AI coding assistant, across 5,414 multinational firms accounting for 38% of the U.S. programming workforce. To identify causal effects, we exploit a natural experiment generated by firms' predetermined software procurement cycles. Early AI-adopting firms hired more workers before the launch of GitHub Copilot and had larger, more technical, and older workforces. After one year, GitHub Copilot adoption reduces quarterly technical hiring by 29% among review-induced adopters, with no effect on separations, overall technical headcount, or vacancy duration. The hiring slowdown is concentrated in the subset of junior technical roles that involve the highest share of coding work. Overall, AI coding assistance causes firms to shift demand towards more experienced workers and roles that pair some coding with broader design responsibilities.
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Raymond, Eleanor Wiske Dillon

item.title: Place-Based Policy from Space: Evidence from Italy's Inner Areas
item.description: arXiv:2611.31100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper evaluates a place-based policy, Italy's National Strategy for Inner Areas (SNAI), using satellite nighttime lights. Targeting structurally fragile and peripheral municipalities, SNAI invests in essential services and economic activities. Staggered difference-in-differences compares 941 funded municipalities with 3,112 eligible controls over 2011--2022. Funding is associated with an expansion of lit area and no detectable change in radiance per lit cell, suggesting that activity extends its footprint rather than intensifying in existing centres. The expansion holds across comparison groups and, descriptively, concentrates at intermediate funding per resident. Annual satellite data can complement slower and coarser statistics.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Caravaggio, Giuseppe Di Renzo, Giuliano Resce, Agapito Emanuele Santangelo, Giulia Valeria Sonzogno

item.title: Optimization of a Solar-Grid Water Supply System with Hydraulic Energy Storage: A Case Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.30019v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given the high cost of grid-scale batteries, other energy storage approaches are needed for developing and low-income regions. Elevated volumes of water are often more economically feasible energy storage options than batteries in these contexts. This paper presents a dual-framework modeling approach for one such energy storage setup: a solar-grid hybrid water supply system in the arid Afar region of Ethiopia. By utilizing an elevated 1,900 m3 water reservoir as a "hydraulic battery," the system replaces traditional electrochemical storage, significantly reducing capital expenditures. Using Python for high-resolution technical simulation and Xendee for economic optimization, the study shows a 55.1% solar fraction and a 10% Internal Rate of Return (IRR). The results confirm that hybrid systems with hydraulic storage offer a financially viable and reliable solution for water access in energy-constrained regions.
item.dc:creator: Mariamawit Gashahun Arega, Jesse Thornburg

item.title: Ancestral origins of environmental (in)attention
item.description: arXiv:2509.09598v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How do ancestral climate experiences shape today's attitudes towards environmental issues? Combining multiple contemporary surveys and ethnic group-level cultural records with a model of cultural selection on costly attention, we show that ancestral climate anomalies have a lasting U-shaped effect on environmental concern. Descendants of groups exposed to the most regular and the most anomalous climates attach greater importance to the environment, with a dip in between; a pattern mirrored in cultural narratives. But why should contemporary environmental concern remain anchored in ancestral climates when lessons about the value of environmental attention can be learned beyond the conditions in which they were initially acquired? Our model shows that because attention is chosen before conditions are realized, cultural selection rewards perceptions that perform well on average without fully correcting their accuracy across conditions. Ancestral climates can thus leave lasting imprints, even as their influence weakens when environments change. The combination of motives to exploit typical conditions and to protect against extremes gives rise to the U-shape, reconciling anthropological accounts that tie environmental concern to regular and to anomalous climates.
item.dc:creator: C\'esar Barilla, Palaash Bhargava

item.title: From Augmentation to Reconstruction: Guiding the AI Disruption to the Good Place
item.description: arXiv:2605.29207v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Artificial intelligence feels omnipresent, yet the disruption many expect has not fully arrived. The main reason is not model capability, nor even the tools built to harness those models. Rather, most organizations are still using AI to accelerate workflows designed for a pre-AI world. We offer a three-stage lens: Augmentation, Automation, and Reconstruction, and argue that the most consequential disruption resides in the third stage where workflows and markets are rebuilt around delegation, machine-to-machine interaction, continuous monitoring, and auditable constraints. Achieving this system-level transformation takes time: it requires trust and accountability infrastructure, machine-legible and interoperable data and interfaces, the design and adoption of these new workflows, and economic incentives that favor reconstruction rather than local optimization: the complementary investments that produce the familiar "productivity J-curve" of general-purpose technologies. We illustrate this transition through examples in consumer markets, education, news, and coding. Finally, we emphasize a normative point: the agentic future is not predetermined. Leaders must both skate to where the puck is going and actively steer it toward a good place, ensuring innovation delivers welfare gains felt by businesses and consumers around the world.
item.dc:creator: David M. Rothschild, Jake M. Hofman, Markus Mobius, Brendan Lucier, Eleanor Dillon, Daniel G. Goldstein, Nicole Immorlica, Aleksandrs Slivkins

item.title: Probabilistic Risk Sensitivity and Loss Aversion in Cumulative Prospect Theory
item.description: arXiv:2606.06652v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops a binary-gamble framework for characterizing risk sensitivity and loss aversion in Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT). The proposed probabilistic risk-sensitivity metric is defined as a probability-threshold ratio that determines acceptance and preference thresholds in choice problems involving either a certain outcome and a binary gamble or two binary gambles. We show how standard notions of symmetric and non-symmetric bet aversion can be recovered within this framework, and we compare the resulting threshold-based conditions with utility premia, probability premia, and Arrow-Pratt curvature measures. The analysis clarifies when these criteria coincide and when they diverge, particularly for increasing aversion conditions, binary gambles with unequal probability distributions, and settings involving probability weighting functions. We also identify technical restrictions that arise when CPT-utility functions are used to represent loss aversion at the reference point. The resulting framework provides a decision-theoretic interpretation of risk sensitivity that is directly tied to probability thresholds and complements existing premium-based approaches.
item.dc:creator: Symeon Vaidanis, Marios Kountouris

item.title: The overlooked price feedback: Why simulations overstate distribution grid peaks from home batteries under real-time pricing
item.description: arXiv:2609.35111v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulation studies of home batteries under real-time pricing commonly find that synchronized charging creates new peaks in distribution grids. Yet all home-battery simulation studies reviewed here treat wholesale prices as exogenous, ignoring the effect of battery dispatch on prices. Charging in low-price hours raises the wholesale price, which dampens the incentive to charge. In equilibrium, charging is spread out across hours. This paper examines how accounting for this feedback changes peaks in local grids. A simulation of household battery dispatch under real-time pricing, calibrated to German data, finds that, if half of households own a battery, exogenous prices raise the coincident import peak by 83 % relative to the no-battery benchmark. With endogenous prices, the same fleet reduces the peak by 6 %. This finding is robust across alternative price functions, price paths, peak measures, and scenario assumptions. While new local peaks remain possible where batteries are geographically concentrated, these results suggest that published studies overstate the local peak-load effects of price-responsive batteries.
item.dc:creator: Lion Hirth

item.title: Linear Demand Systems are Consistent with Discrete Choice
item.description: arXiv:2610.13785v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Aggregate linear demand systems can be micro-founded by a population of heterogeneous consumers making discrete choices. They can also be extended to incorporate income effects. I prove these results and show how to structurally estimate this class of models using only market-level data. The distribution of heterogeneous consumer preferences is recovered by disciplining the corner solutions with aggregate terms only. This approach allows for the same richness of Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes (1995) [BLP] while retaining the analytical and computational advantages of linear demand: it does not require exogenously fixing market size, allows for heterogeneity in choice sets, and results in a flexible substitution matrix which varies endogenously as different consumers enter/exit the market. The discrete-choice microfoundation facilitates welfare analysis and the flexible measurement of markups an cost pass-throughs, among a wide range of other applications.
item.dc:creator: Afonso Rodrigues

item.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Forecast Treatment Effects in Economics?
item.description: arXiv:2610.38883v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: I use LLMs to forecast treatment effects from pre-registrations and pre-analysis plans, evaluating forecasts against results released after the models' cut-off dates. The screened sample includes 1,459 questions from 36 papers. For the most recent time period and model, the median absolute error is 0.053 SD, the average absolute error is 0.098 SD, and the MSE is 0.021, falling to 0.015 after adjusting for sampling variance where standard errors are available. Forecasts substantially outperform benchmarks predicting zero or other papers' mean effects. These results suggest considerable scope for forecasts to inform policy and research.
item.dc:creator: Eva Vivalt

item.title: The Rise of Agents and the Labor Market
item.description: arXiv:2611.27210v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We provide the first economy-wide and cross-AI model evidence on the effects of agentic AI on labor demand. We combine proprietary OpenRouter data covering about two quadrillion tokens of realized AI consumption (2 percent of global AI token consumption) across more than 400 AI models, including 1.1 quadrillion agentic tokens, with the full text of 34.8 million U.S. job postings for public firms from Lightcast. We compute our measure of firm-level exposure to aggregate agentic AI consumption (agentic beta) using the comovement of U.S. public firms' stock returns with realized weekly aggregate agentic AI token consumption. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm's exposure to agentic AI predicts 2.11 percent lower growth in job postings over the next six months and 3.20 percent over nine months. We then conduct an event study based on the release of Claude Code 2.0, which significantly expanded the capabilities of AI agents, and show that a one-standard-deviation higher pre-release exposure to agentic AI predicts 4.73 percent lower posting growth over six months post the release. Furthermore, we show that the decrease in job postings is concentrated among non-senior jobs and is statistically insignificant for senior jobs. In contrast, we find no statistically significant relation between broad AI realized consumption exposure and subsequent job posting growth once agentic exposure is controlled for. Finally, we validate our market-implied agentic exposure measure using independent evidence from firms' mentions of AI deployment in securities filings and earnings calls.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Borri, Anton Cheremukhin, Yukun Liu, Aleh Tsyvinski

item.title: DeepVoting: Learning and Improving Voting Rules with Fine-Tuning
item.description: arXiv:2408.13630v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recently, social choice theory has been found broadly useful for AI alignment and evaluation, often based on the axiomatic properties for combining preferences provided by social choice functions. However, for many sets of axioms, functions which never violate the axioms are known to not exist, e.g., Arrow's Impossibility Theorem. Recent work on learning novel rules to minimize axiom violations shows the effectiveness of machine learning but explores a limited class of axioms. In this work we show the effectiveness of standard social choice data structures as features for learning existing voting rules, resulting in networks that have better accuracy than past approaches while using an order of magnitude fewer parameters. Subsequently, we develop a process for adding axiomatic properties to existing voting rules. By building novel axiomatic loss functions we are able to use transfer learning to fine-tune existing voting rules in a way that quantitatively preserves their original behaviour while also exhibiting strong adherence to previously absent axiomatic properties, resulting in novel voting rules that are closer to the impossibility frontier than those in the machine learning or theoretical literature.
item.dc:creator: Leonardo Matone, Ben Abramowitz, Ben Armstrong, Avinash Balakrishnan, Nicholas Mattei

item.title: Decarbonization without deindustrialization in future pathways for European industry
item.description: arXiv:2510.08199v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Decarbonizing European industry while maintaining international competitiveness are two central objectives of European Union (EU) policy, yet they may conflict. This study investigates trade-offs between these goals across alternative industrial production pathways, from continued decline to policy-driven reindustrialization, focusing on steel, cement, methanol, ammonia, and high-value chemicals. Using an extended PyPSA-Eur energy system model with detailed process-level representation, we compare domestic low-carbon production costs against imported alternatives and evaluate three policy strategies: intra-European relocation, selective green intermediate imports, and targeted subsidies. Deep industrial decarbonization is technically feasible, with electrification playing a central role, but cost competitiveness peaks during the investment-intensive transition phase around 2040. Intra-European relocation delivers limited savings and faces significant real-world constraints. Strategic imports of green intermediates substantially reduce system costs while preserving downstream industrial activity. Overall, European industrial policy should prioritize decarbonizing existing capacity, leveraging green intermediate imports to retain high-value domestic production, supported by targeted, time-limited public support.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Di Bella, A., Seibold, T., Brown, T., & Tavoni, M. (2026). Decarbonization without deindustrialization in future pathways for European industry. Cell Reports Sustainability, 100837
item.dc:creator: Alice Di Bella, Toni Seibold, Tom Brown, Massimo Tavoni

item.title: Fair outputs, Biased Internals: Causal Potency and Asymmetry of Latent Bias in LLMs for High-Stakes Decisions
item.description: arXiv:2605.15217v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Instruction-tuned language models exhibit behavioural fairness in high-stakes decisions while retaining biased associations in their internal representations. However, whether these suppressed representations can affect model outputs - and whether such causal potency is symmetric across demographic groups - remains unknown. We investigate the use of open-weight models for mortgage underwriting using matched applications that differ only in racially-associated names and reveal a critical disconnect: models show no output-level bias, yet retain and amplify demographic representations across model layers. Through activation steering and novel cross-layer interventions, we demonstrate that this suppressed information is decision-relevant: when reinjected at critical layers, it produces near-complete decision reversals. Critically, this latent bias is asymmetric - steering interventions affect decisions in one demographic direction, while producing minimal effects in reverse - and susceptible to adversarial prompt engineering and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These findings demonstrate that behavioural audits focused on outputs are insufficient: fair outputs can mask exploitable internal biases. They also motivate dual-layer testing frameworks combining output evaluation with representational analysis for AI governance in high-stakes decisions.
item.dc:creator: Jagdish Tripathy, Marcus Buckmann

item.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.22033v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.
item.dc:creator: Adi Krishnamoorthy, X. Y. Han
